# Inject external credentials with the Credential Injection Processor

External credential injection authenticates approved external HTTP calls at a Consul terminating gateway. Provider credentials stay at the gateway that needs them instead of being distributed to agent applications. External Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are the primary use case. The same mechanism works for other external HTTP APIs that accept a bearer token or API key, such as a hosted model inference API.

@include '../../../global/partials/alerts/beta.mdx'

The Credential Injection Processor implements this feature. It runs as a sidecar on the terminating gateway and receives credentials from a Vault Agent sidecar or a Kubernetes Secret. To configure it, refer to [Configure external credential injection](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/credential-injection/configure).

@include 'alerts/enterprise-alert.mdx'

## Introduction

External MCP servers and APIs often require a bearer token or API key, even when the caller already has a Consul workload identity. Mesh authorization and provider credentials solve different problems. Mesh authorization decides which workloads can call the external service. The provider credential authenticates the gateway to the external provider.

Consul and the credential source each supply part of the request:

| Supplier | What it provides |
| --- | --- |
| Consul configuration | The approved destination, mesh policy, external TLS settings, and a non-secret credential-binding identifier |
| Vault or a Kubernetes Secret | The credential for each binding, with its rotation deadline and expiry |

Consul never stores provider credentials in its configuration, and Vault never publishes them to Consul. The Credential Injection Processor joins the binding from Consul with the credential from the source at the moment of the call.

## How it works

1. An in-mesh caller sends a request to the external service through a configured upstream. The caller can be the MCP Sidecar routing an approved tool call, or an agent workload calling an external API.
1. The service mesh carries the request to the terminating gateway. Workload authentication and service intentions apply before any credential is added.
1. Consul writes the credential-binding identifier into the gateway's route configuration. Envoy passes the identifier to the local Credential Injection Processor.
1. The processor removes any authentication or binding headers the caller sent, then sets the one authentication header configured for the binding. Envoy rejects any other change from the processor, so the processor cannot alter the destination, path, or route.
1. The gateway connects to the external service over TLS and verifies its certificate against the configured CA and server name. The gateway forwards the request only when both the route and its credential are usable.

The [Govern tool access](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/architecture#govern-tool-access) diagram on the architecture page shows this path for an MCP tool call.

### Requirements for each external service

- **TLS.** Consul rejects a terminating gateway configuration that enables credential injection for a service without a CA file and a DNS server name (SNI). A provider credential is never sent over plaintext.
- **HTTP.** The external service must use an HTTP-based protocol.
- **One supported header.** Each binding injects exactly one of the following headers:

| Header | Value sent to the external service |
| --- | --- |
| `authorization` | `Bearer <credential>` |
| `authorization` | `apikey <credential>` |
| `x-api-key` | `<credential>` |
| `x-goog-api-key` | `<credential>` |
| `api-key` | `<credential>` |

## What operators control

Operators bind each logical destination to an approved external endpoint, an authentication header, and a credential. Callers control none of it. A caller cannot select a Vault path, provider account, credential-binding identifier, header name, or external TLS server name.

Binding settings come only from Consul configuration. The gateway removes binding headers that a caller sends, so a caller cannot redirect an approved credential to a host of its choosing.

Only the processes that need a credential can read it:

- Applications and the MCP Sidecar never receive provider credentials.
- The Credential Injection Processor reads rendered credentials, but not the Vault Agent's authentication token.

## Credential sources

| Source | How credentials arrive |
| --- | --- |
| Vault | Default. A Vault Agent sidecar authenticates to Vault with the gateway's Kubernetes service account. It renders each credential to a memory-backed volume that only the Credential Injection Processor reads. Credentials are never written to persistent storage. The Vault Agent connects to Vault over HTTPS and verifies the server certificate against a configured CA. |
| Kubernetes Secret | Consul mounts a Kubernetes Secret read-only into the Credential Injection Processor. This source is weaker than Vault. |

To choose a source and store credentials, refer to [Choose a credential source](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/credential-injection/configure#choose-a-credential-source).

## Rotation and expiry

To rotate a credential in Vault, write a new version of its secret. The Credential Injection Processor picks up the new version without a gateway restart. It validates each update and swaps the active credential without exposing a partly written value. An older version never replaces a newer accepted one.

Each credential has a rotation deadline and an optional expiry. A credential stops being usable shortly before the earlier of the two, even if Vault is unavailable and no newer credential arrives. A Vault outage does not extend how long the gateway uses a cached credential.

When a binding has no usable credential because it is missing, invalid, or expired, the gateway fails that call closed instead of forwarding it without authentication. A problem with one binding does not affect other bindings.

A running processor does not mean that every binding has a usable credential. Monitor each binding through the processor's logs. Refer to [Verify the configuration](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/credential-injection/configure#verify-the-configuration).

## Security

- Provider credentials and Vault tokens stay out of agent configuration, Consul configuration, proxy configuration snapshots, logs, traces, and error messages.
- The processor can change only the configured authentication header. It cannot change the route or turn off external TLS verification.
- Binding status, policy outcomes, and rotation failures are logged without secret values.
- Caller authorization still applies when a credential is available.

## Limitations

External credential injection covers external HTTP services, including MCP servers and other APIs, that use a [supported authentication header](#requirements-for-each-external-service) with a credential from Vault or a Kubernetes Secret.

It does not cover the following:

- Authentication to managed model providers
- OAuth delegation. For user delegation, refer to [On-behalf-of delegation](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/identity).
- Request signing or client-certificate authentication
- Secret managers other than Vault
- Non-HTTP MCP transports
- Wildcard service names in the terminating gateway configuration
- OpenShift
